utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they allow us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I want you to turn your attention to paragraph 23 of the same time document. The middle of the page. Paragraph 23. Middle of the page. When you talk about not knowing any of the -- about the relationship between Croatian police and the military. This is talking about getting stopped at the check-point in Otric. "We drove through the fields to get around a check-point the same day we were stopped."

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in fact, you and Mr. -- I believe you were with Mr. Martins at this time, got around this check-point quite easily, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Depends how you see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you tell me --

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: We went through the fields, yes. So we went there. But still we were being stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After you got stopped, you and Mr. Martins --

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yeah, but we took another way, another road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. After you got stopped, you and Mr. Martins got around this check-point by driving through fields.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if civilians who were engaged in some type of improper conduct wanted to get around that check-point, they could have done the same thing that you and Mr. Martins did. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In fact, when you were going through this area you were dealing with a lot of rumours about crimes as well as particular criminal events, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: What do you mean by rumours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to paragraph 5. I'll give you an example. If we can go to the bottom of page 2 of 22 on the same document, paragraph 5. If you read that bottom part of the page. "I usually went on patrols with Luis Martins and one interpreter. We patrolled daily, seven days a week. Our general practice when we patrolled was to stop in the villages that we visited and look around. For example, we would look inside wells because we heard that people were sometimes put in wells. We never found any bodies in wells." Now the bodies being thrown in wells was a rumour that was rampant in the area, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you found no evidence during your patrols to support that?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the actual investigations by the Gracac police department, again, you noted that they could have done more to patrol and that you weren't getting the information that you needed. But let me -- before I ask you questions in that regard, I would like to show you a document, 65 ter 2091. And this is an UN CIVPOL Sector South report. And if you can take a look at this, report, I believe you referred to this in one of your statements, and if we can go ten pages in. Now, we were talking about the ability or you were on direct examination talking about the ability of the Gracac police department to do more. And let us look at the second paragraph at the top of that page, where it notes: "Regularly joint patrols with CRO POL, Croatian police, have tried to be established. Some of these have been cancelled because CRO POL did not have enough police officers." Now, were you aware of that fact when you were down there that the Croatian police, the civilian police, did not have enough police officers?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Not as I remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the first page of this document, at the bottom of the page. Talking about patrols and cooperation. "In this level, it seem that the cooperation is good. However, many joint patrols have been cancelled due to lack of police officers and vehicles." Now, were you aware of both of those shortages on behalf of the Croatian police when you were in Sector South and Sector North, or especially Gracac, that is, the paucity or lack of police officers and vehicles?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Not what I remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also mentioned to us that -- and it says in your report that you weren't getting information back on investigations. Do you recall that generally?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes, I remember my report also about that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we can -- you actually discuss it for just reference points, Your Honours, in paragraph 19 of P -- of P774. Let us look at some documents, and if I can first bring up P425. Now, as we're bringing this document up, ma`am, were you aware that crime was being investigated in the Gracac area, not by the police station in Gracac but by the arm of the civilian police in Zadar? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Not as I remember today. I remember about a judge mentioned in reports coming to the area. But not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn -- this is P425, if we can go to the next page. This is a -- a situation where you came with others, as you can see, you're at the top, your name is at the top. And about midway it notes that with regard to the first homicide of Milan Marcetic that one commissioner and one judge from Zadar came to this place and then with their order the police took the body to Zadar. Now, from that, ma`am, did you inquire whether or not this was being investigated in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were writing this report and you were getting this information about a commissioner and a judge coming to the village to investigate, did you inquire whether this crime was being investigated in Zadar as opposed to in the Gracac police department?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, likewise, with the next homicide at the bottom of the page, you likewise received the same information on the second death that, again, a commissioner and a judge came from Zadar to examine the scene and to examine -- and to take the body, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes. Looks like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that when you made this statement as to whether or not something is being investigated certainly to your satisfaction, it is important to know who exactly is doing the investigation?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes. But the incidents were brought up to the Gracac police and if I remember it from other reports, I think they have mentioned that it should be investigated by Zadar. I think so. But still, why didn't we receive any answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, ma`am, when you received the information that this was being investigated from -- in Zadar, did you make inquiries of the criminal investigation unit in Zadar as to what was happening with this investigation?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact procedure how it was done. Of course we asked for an answer but how it was done, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us turn to the next page which documents in the same -- in this same exhibit which documents yet further investigation, were you aware that individuals were -- from the village were brought down to Zadar in an attempt to identify any -- or a potential perpetrator of this crime. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember this, no. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of any incident when you were in the Gracac area or in the Obrovac area, where the police department solved -- a Croatian police department entity solved a crime based on information that CIVPOL this provided?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Not as I remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go back to the report that we had up previously; that would be 65 ter 2091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I don't find that on the list of the Prosecution. You neither tendered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will tender it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will tender this. At this time I will tender 65 ter 2091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter P2091 would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would be Exhibit D740, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D740 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to ten pages in on that document. And about midway down, notes on the meeting of 24/10/1995 in Benkovac: "24/10/1995 in Benkovac, chief policija Mr. Nica, K-n-e-z, Knez, informed that because of the information given to CRO POL by UN CIVPOL about the number of the plates of a car seen in Gosici village, they had solved a murder case ..." Now, did you know about that, ma`am?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to say, as you sit here, you have no idea of investigations that were being conducted by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia during your stay in the former Yugoslavia. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Well, I assume so, unless the chief of investigation in Gracac didn't inform us. I don't know why he would not inform us at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question to you is, ma`am, do you know what the Republic of Croatia Minister of Interior were investigating, what crimes they were investigating?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me cover a couple of points, if I may. And if we could just bring back up 65 ter -- excuse me, P780. This is a document that was discussed by counsel during your direct examination. And it notes that this is the situation where the police were protecting the graveyard. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these graves -- were these bodies being buried in conformity with humanitarian law; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Before that question is asked, perhaps a foundation could be established as to the witness's knowledge of humanitarian law and burial of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just asking if she knows if they were buried in accordance with humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that in answer to Ms. Gustafson's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- objection? She says it needs --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't believe it needs a -- I think the question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You consider it for every witness just to have knowledge of humanitarian law in such a way that you could answer this question? Doesn't need expertise there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, to a degree of a person being in the area that is involved in that. The knowledge of whether or not bodies are being buried in conformity with humanitarian law is not a quantum leap as to whether or not she knows, but I'll make the -- I will lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess, if she's -- it has been represented she is testifying and reporting observations of violations of humanitarian law so I suppose the foundation question was answered in her direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, if I'm expected to report on the health situation of a population, I'm not yet a medical doctor. Nevertheless, I can describe certain observations I make. You offered kindly enough, Mr. Kehoe, to lay a foundation. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know how bodies are supposed to be buried in conformity with humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you looked at the Gracac cemetery and you saw these bodies, do you have any idea where these bodies came from?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There was a 24-hour guard protecting this area, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Not from the beginning but at the end, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go -- as of your report on the 11th of September of 1995, there 's a 24-hour a-day-guard of that cemetery, right?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: At this time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is taking place when, you have testified, that looting and other crimes are taking place in the area by people coming back into the area. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This 24-hour guard at the Gracac cemetery is guarding this graveyard at a time when your reports reflect that people are telling you that a variety of crimes are takes place. Isn't that right? Happening at the same time.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Given that situation, Ms. Malm, is -- don`t you believe it is eminently reasonable for the Croatian police department to take the wise course and protect bodies, especially Serb bodies, which may be in this cemetery? Don't you think that is perfectly reasonable for them to do?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I didn't question this -- this check-point, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is, in an area that you, from your reports attest, people are telling you many different crimes are taking place, is it not eminently reasonable for the Croatian police department to put a 24-hour guard on a Serb cemetery to protect those bodies? Isn't that reasonable?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to one last area and you, in your reports, have told us or you have admitted into evidence some reports on some killing incidents. Now, all of the information you received about people either dying or being killed in the area, let me clarify, that you never witnessed any killing. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the information that you have in your reports was told to you by other individuals.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And once you received this information, UN CIVPOL did not conduct an investigation on its own, did they?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you -- the information you received you passed on to the Croatian civilian police.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't pass it on to the Croatian military structure, did you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you write these reports, you are not attesting to the accuracy of the information that is given to you, you are just writing down what people are telling you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That is correct. But if I would feel that something is wrong with the person and something is not correct, I would mention it, because that is what I do in Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But, ma'am, as you said before, you did no independent investigation after this information was given to you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now let us talk about a few items that have been received in evidence. Let's go to P795, if we may, first. Now, this is an incident in Zrmanja, 25 September 1995, concerning the bodies being decomposed with identification very difficult. You don't know anything about how this individual died, do you? The circumstances under which he died, or they died, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P251. This is a report concerning an individual by the name of Gojko Komazec found at the side of the road. You identified three bullets to the stomach. You likewise have no knowledge concerning the circumstances of this individual's death either, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is information you received in -- again in Zrmanja on the 6th of September, 1995, concerning two Serbian men shot by Croatian soldiers "during some of the first days of the attack." I ask you the same question: You have no idea concerning the circumstances of the death of these two men either, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. Not more than I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you don't know, for instance, whether or not they were combatants at the time they died, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. I only know what's in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to P789. This is a report of 9 -- excuse me, of 6 September 1995, in the village of Palanka and it notes that a Serb -- it's in the second paragraph, the individual Brkic, Dusan, was shot by Croatian soldiers. Brkic was dressed in military uniform. By the time of the murder he had no weapons. Now, you use the term "murder" there. Do you know anything of the circumstances of the death of Mr. Dusan Brkic?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, not more than is in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, you use the term "murder." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now why did you use the term "murder"?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Probably that's why she told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could bring up 65 ter 251. This is it the report of -- autopsy reports of Dr. Baccard, a Prosecution expert. And if we could go to page 116, and it's -- the number at the top, the date stamp number is 3455583. 55583, please. My colleague says try page 33. No. 3455583. 55583, I'm sorry, if I said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, this is the autopsy of Dusan Brkic, the number is GO7/0025. We identify it as Dusan Brkic, so it is in the report but it's also in a filing, the most recent clarification schedule of the Prosecution. If I may proceed, Judge, I can just read it as opposed to just going to the document. We're going to see the document down the line, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm informed it's 65 ter 471. Page 116. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The individual that is discussed at the bottom of this page, if we can just blow up the bottom. The Prosecution expert, Ms. Malm, in the bottom of the page dealing with Mr. Brkic notes that: "I agree with the conclusion of Dr. Blazanovic's report. The clothing examination showed several large defects on the front side and the left sleeve of the shirt with edges were burnt. This aspect being consistent with the hypothesis of explosion." That is reaffirmed by Dr. Baccard subsequently. Now, when you received this information and this person said you were murder -- that this person told that you this individual was murdered, did they mention to you that he been hit by some type of explosion?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. Only what was in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go back to that P789 just briefly. Now, looking at this report, Ms. Malm, where once again Mr. Brkic was in a military uniform and the Prosecution's expert maintains that the hypothesis of death is consistent with explosion. Does that indicate to you as a law enforcement officer that this individual was not murdered but died in combat?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I just wrote what I was told from these villagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you don't know anything else other than just what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. If I had been told something about explosions, I would have written it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Malm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, have I no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no questions on behalf of Mr. Cermak, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have some questions. I'd just like to get set up for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: All set, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, with respect to your reporting, what kind of training did you have before you came an UN CIVPOL officer in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: It was a week in Stockholm. But I can't remember exactly how was the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you have specifically as far as your training is concerned? Did you learn about the area, did you learn about the people? What -- if you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I think we were told about the history about the former Yugoslavia. Probably some kind of report writing. Of course, we were not aware of the situation we would end up in. So I would say that we were not really prepared or trained for what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that training lasted for how long?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: A week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that was in Sweden?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then did you first come to Zagreb then?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any training in Zagreb at all?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Did you meet at all with any Croatian counterparts in Zagreb to learn about the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's fair to state that as far as you know, before you started your position as an UN CIVPOL officer in Croatia, you had no knowledge of what the structure of the Croatian police was?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And I guess it is similarly true that no one gave you any instruction as to what the general background and scope of Croatian criminal law was?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in -- your first posting after Zagreb was where? Sector North, you said?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes, Sector North. Immediately I was, as far as I remember, I was in Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P774, if that could be called up, please. I'm not sure if the witness has that, Ms. Gustafson. If she's got it in front of her, might make it a little bit easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: She doesn't, but I have a copy of it. If she can be given her statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Malm, I have asked for the exhibit to be called up on the screen, but I wanted you to have a copy of it to make it easier for you to follow. If you could take a look at paragraph 8, please. The second sentence of paragraph 8 says that, and I'm referring to the -- when you were in Knin, that you: "Never personally observed Croatian soldiers putting houses on fire, but people in the villages and hamlets often told us that Croatian soldiers looted and burnt houses. I made reports about the quantity of houses burnt when I visited villages. Two of these reports are referenced in the table of CIVPOL reports below."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer to 65 ter 4765, please, if we could put that up. And while we're waiting for it come up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Malm, when you say in your statement the quantity of houses you're talking about numbers?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say quantity of houses burnt when you visited villages, you were talking about numbers of houses?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Quantity. We estimated the percentage. That's how we did it. We didn't exactly count one, two, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So when we have up on our screen now, 65 ter 4765, this is villages and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, in order to make it possible for those who will later look at the transcript, that is provisionally assigned number P784.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P774, which is now on the screen right now, provisionally assigned, is entitled villages and hamlets visited 28/8/1995. Is that your signature on the bottom right there?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that signature is dated 1997?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, here you have various villages listed that you visited on that particular date and obviously there is no numbers that you put on those estimates. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. It says all houses burned, for example, for Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And for example, in Bratiskovici, it says: "Most houses intact, just a few burned." Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you have further down: "20 per cent burned in Djakici, right?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You haven't given us any estimate of what that means in terms of quantifiable numbers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So when you use the term "quantity" in your statement, P774, you don't actually give us a specific number?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you made reports to the civilian police in Gracac, was that basically the place where you reported anything that you saw that appeared to you to be a crime?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, it was the only place I went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of what the territorial boundaries and divisions were of the Croatian police districts immediately after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite possible, is it not that you reported things to the Gracac police station that were not within their district or jurisdiction to investigate. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you -- in your statement and we'll go to P774 again, please. Paragraph 23, and I'll wait for it to get on the screen so the Chamber can follow. Paragraph 23, you were talking about check-points. And in the second sentence it says: "In general, I don't know anything about the relationship between the Croatian police and the military." I guess following those lines, you could not tell us whether the civilian police had any jurisdiction over men in military uniforms, can you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us whether the military police were the only ones who had jurisdiction to deal with alleged crimes committed by persons in military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, you're referring to men in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from your last question, not from the one before that, you suggest that military police had jurisdiction with alleged crimes committed by persons in military uniforms. Now, I do understand from a lot of cross-examination that the last thing you could conclude from the fact that someone is in a military uniform is that he is -- that he is a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, could you explain to me what is the basis that military police has jurisdiction over civilians dressed in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, that's not the question that I asked, whether there were civilians in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do understand. But you put as part of the question that military police had jurisdiction over those who were in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess it was a foundation -- it was really a foundation question, Your Honour. I was asking her whether she knew whether or not the military police had jurisdiction over people in military uniforms, and if that's not how it's in the transcript, then I asked the question very poorly. So I can re-ask the question if that is problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked whether the military police were the only one who had jurisdiction to deal with alleged crimes committed by personnel in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. And that was really a foundation question as to whether she knew that existed or not. So I'm not representing it as a fact, I'm asking her whether she knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a rather complex question apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess I can try to split it and make it little more simple, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Malm, do you know what role, if any, the military police had immediately after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So do you know what their jurisdiction was?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The same thing with the civilian police. Do you know what role they had after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Civilian police, I suppose, is there to protect lives and property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what jurisdiction they had, immediately after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And it's fair to state that you did not learn from anyone what their structure was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you had said that you reported your observations to the Croatian police in Gracac and you were a bit critical that the Croatian police chief or the Croatian police in Gracac did not report back to you. It's true, is it not, that under the UN CIVPOL mandate, an agreement with Croatian, the Croatian police had no obligation to report anything to you after you gave them information. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- can you point me to any document, any agreement that you're aware of that states the Croatian police had any obligation after you gave them information to report back to you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, even though did you report violations to the Croatian police, you stated that you didn't report everything. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your primary obligation was to report crimes to the local police after you observed them, as an UN CIVPOL member?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what was the rules today. But we found it proper to inform the police since they were ones who should investigate it. So if we found something seriously happened, then we went there. If the time was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it fair to state that because on many or most occasions they didn't report back to you, you assume that they did nothing about investigating those reports you gave to them?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I think it was because of -- of the meetings where I told that I couldn't show any results and also because we saw that the crime was still going on. On the fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Other crime. But not the crime that you necessarily would have reported in the first instance. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. I mean other crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So I guess it's fair to say that with respect to the things that you did report to the civilian police, you don't know one way or the other what investigation was done, whether anyone was charged or convicted with any crimes that you reported to them. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we were not informed about any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to go into the areas of Sveti Rok or Lovinac during your patrols in and around Gracac, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Lovinac and?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sveti Rok.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Lovinac sounds familiar but I'm not sure. I have to refer to reports in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there aren't any reports in your materials regarding Lovinac or Sveti Rok as those were areas that were primarily before 1991 occupied by Croats and had been destroyed, and I was just wondering if you had any opportunity to go in those areas.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember. Then we have to look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement, P774, paragraph 20, you talk in the lower -- the third-last line discussing the report which is entitled, Team Obrovac assessment of cooperation with CRO POL from October 1995 until today. It says: "The report states that cooperation between the Croatian police and UN CIVPOL was 'good' during the period. I don't think it should be characterized as 'good' because we never received any information from them." And, again, I'm going to back to the discussion I had with you regarding receiving information from the Croatian civilian police. Simply because you did not receive any information does not mean that anything -- that nothing was done to investigate crimes by the Croatian civilian police. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: The way you put it, could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the report was written by whom?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Which report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The report that's referred to in paragraph 20, the Team Obrovac assessment. Was that a joint report which had input from all CIVPOL officers or was that one person that wrote the report?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Can I see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's D740.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the cover page of the document it appears to be written by a name -- person named Per Roed. Is that familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this report came out?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I just think that the specific report Counsel is referring to is page 10 of this larger document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- and it might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are separate reports in one bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go to page 10 of this document. Thanks, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is simply entitled, Team Obrovac Assessment. And I guess before I ask you any specific questions about the report, you said you had read the Team Obrovac assessment dated 19 November. When did you read it?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: This one, I think, I read in the Prosecutor's office. I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When -- when in the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Six weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So that is the first time that you saw this particular report?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it is 13 years ago all this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sure. I understand that and I don't begrudge you that at all. You -- do you recall yourself having any input into the items that are filled in in this report?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in this report, because I reported to the team leader, Lennart Widen, and he informed the Knin HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if anyone, it's your recollection that Mr. Widen would have been the one who would have contributed to this report?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Ms. Gustafson any further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: About two minutes, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You were just asked a few questions about cooperation with the Gracac policija and one of the things you were asked was whether it was possible that you reported crimes that were not within the jurisdiction of the Gracac policija. I'd like to ask you this: Do you remember ever being given the answer from the police that the incident you were reporting was not within their jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the division of the territory into municipalities, the Gracac municipality versus the Knin municipality? If you're not --

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In general, were you reporting incidents to the Gracac policija that occurred in the Gracac area or were you reporting incidents that occurred outside the Gracac area?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: In the Gracac area, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were also asked about whether you -- whether the Croatian police had any obligation to report back to you. In your meetings with the Gracac policija, did they ever refuse to give you answers on the basis that they had no -- that there were not required to report to UN CIVPOL?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And one last question. Back to an earlier question you were asked by Mr. Kehoe about armed people in civilian clothes and you say -- you said in answer: "I remember seeing one man in civilian clothes running from a house and he was carrying a hunting rifle." Is that the only armed person in civilian clothes you remember seeing during your time there, or do you remember others?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's the only one I can remember today. This clear picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Malm, I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one is a follow-up question to a question that was put to you by Mr. Kehoe. He asked you: "You never went and talked to these people and say, Why are you taking" I think it reads, the transcript is not very clear, "product from an individual house and putting it in yours." And then your answer, although appears not quite clearly, was: "No, not as far as I can remember." The question was related to what you described as looting. Did you ever see, apart from seeing goods taken out of houses that such goods were then taken into private houses, after that?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I remember today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question would be about those who were guarding the graveyard where you told us, and it is also in a report. In the report, it reads: "When we had been in the yard for a few minutes, a policija officer showed up. He informed us that no one is allowed to enter the graveyard without permission from policija." Did you have any conversation with this policija officer who said that you were not allowed in the graveyard?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I remember we stopped and we spoke to him, but I don't remember exactly how the conversation went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you explained to him what your role and your position was?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell me if you do not remember, but did it come to your mind that what the police officer was doing, which is not allowing you to come to the graveyard, that that was done for the purpose of not allowing you to commit any crime, such as looting?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No. I don't understand why he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently, he was there - at least that's how I understand your testimony - to keep persons off, and that is also what I read from the report --

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- keep people off from entering the graveyard. Did you gain, at the time, any impression as why he was keeping people off from entering the graveyard?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any questions triggered by the questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the -- Ms. Malm, just a few brief questions with regard to the goods that were taken. Do you have any idea where those people were taking those goods?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: No idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, this graveyard situation, and the guard that was there, was it a fact that this -- this policeman that was there was preventing anybody from going in there without authorisation? Isn't that what he told you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: I don't remember what he told me but I remember from the report that he told us that not even the Serbs are allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So from the report that you got, nobody was allowed into the graveyard without authorisation.

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: That's the impression I have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One last question on this. One last question on this, ma'am. As a police officer, if you receive an order not to allow people to come into an area, you as a police officer aren't going to allow anybody in with without authorisation, are you?

utterances.speaker: LAILA MALM
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Ms. Malm, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered questions put to you, both by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Ms. Malm out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties, meanwhile, have received a list from Madam Registrar, in which we find eight documents already admitted into evidence, one still MFI, that is P778. Are there any objections against the other items appearing on this list, some of them already put to the witness, that is, on this list, numbers ten up to and including 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so. We've been through these documents and schedules several times but there has been a degree of confusion, at least for me, because there have been three different lists. If I could just -- at the next break just go through these particular documents and I can have an answer for you at that juncture if that is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will do that. We'll give you an opportunity to -- and I take it that other Defence counsel then will also go through the list. Ms. Gustafson, I don't know whether you are still with us after the break, where we expect the next witness to be called. Will you be in court?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I can make myself available, Your Honour, if that is helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no objections, the Chamber will decide on admission of these documents. Perhaps if there are any objections, if you would be stand by so as to be in a position to respond to that. Perhaps there could already by an informal communication between Defence counsel and Ms. Gustafson, how alert she should be on any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just tell counsel, whoever's here. I don't anticipate them to be any problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a very practical problem. If there's any objection, I take it that not just any of Ms. Gustafson's colleagues could respond to that, and since I would like to keep the MFI list as short as possible, if there's any objection I would expect you to inform Ms. Gustafson during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I said, as a matter of fact, in relation to P792 and P793, that I would expect them to be admitted into evidence since they were used by the first Defence team. I, however, did not formally admit them into evidence. At least I'm not quite sure about this. We'll deal with the list after the break. We will have a break. Ms. Gustafson, I do understand that the next witness to be called is available?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to first deal with the exhibits. We had already P774 up till and including 777, in evidence. P778 was marked for identification. The Prosecution is invited to -- to redact P778, preferably then agree with the Defence whether the way of redacting meets the concerns expressed. Of course, if there's still disagreement then, of course, the Chamber will decide. P779 up to and including P782 were admitted into evidence already. Madam Registrar, could you please deal with the next nine documents provisionally -- where provisionally exhibit numbers were assigned. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just discussed it with Ms. Gustafson, from P783 to P797 there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need to everything with full accuracy on the record. Madam Registrar, if would you read the 65 ter numbers and the numbers provisionally assigned to these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit numbers have been assigned as follows: 65 ter 5369, Exhibit number P783. 65 ter 4765, Exhibit number P784. 65 ter 5375, Exhibit number P785. 65 ter 2560, Exhibit number P786. 65 ter 2565, Exhibit number P787. 65 ter 5383, Exhibit number P788. 65 ter 3188, Exhibit number P789. 65 ter 5376, Exhibit number P790. 65 ter 5378, P781.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you misspoke and that you wanted to make it P791, the last one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then P792 and P793, as has been checked during the break by Madam Registrar, are already admitted into evidence. We'll then continue, Madam Registrar, with number 21 on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the final four documents are 65 ter 5381, that would be Exhibit number P794. 65 ter 1823, Exhibit number P795. 65 ter 924, Exhibit number P796. And, finally, 65 ter 5382, Exhibit number P797.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. P783 up to and including P791 are admitted into evidence. The next two numbers, 792 and 793 were already admitted. P794 up to and including P797 are admitted into evidence. The Chamber would like to hear from the parties on P778 later this week. I think that would not be -- would be sufficient time. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Good evening, Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Liborius. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The next is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. Mr. Liborius, you are not a native English-speaking person. If you have ever any problem in either understanding the questions put to you in this language or in the -- in answering those questions in this language, please inform me immediately. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please make a pause after my question, and it is usually best to follow the cursor on your screen. As soon as it has stopped moving, it is safe for you to answer. Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: My name is Soren Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall giving five witness statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, the first dated 2nd November, 1995; this is 65 ter 5409. The second on 21st August, 1997; 65 ter 5410. The third on the 11th and 12th October 2005; which is 65 ter 5411. The fourth on 19 and 20 May, and 19 and 20 June 2008; this is 65 ter 5412. And the last and final, dated 6th September 2008; this is 65 ter 5439. Do you recall having given these five statements to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the assistance of the usher, I would like to give these five statements, hard copies to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review all five of those statements prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I did review them. However, the statement dated 5 and 6 September 2008 does not carry my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if 65 ter 5439 could be pulled up on the screen. Because I did print, I think, the version that's been disclosed over the weekend. And if we can look at the first page, and perhaps you discover your signature.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: There's no page currently available.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we have to wait a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have a signed copy right now of the witness statement. If that could be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no problem, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I take it that the fifth statement will be uploaded shortly in e-court. Now, for the time being, in reviewing these statements, Mr. Liborius, can you tell the Court whether they accurately reflect what you told the investigators at the time those statements were taken?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether all five statements taken together are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you were questioned today about the matters contained in these statements, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time I'd like to move the five statements into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know we made a filing, however, I do wish to reserve my position until the end of the cross-examination, of the position on the Gotovina Defence on the statements we believe, after reviewing everything, that there may be a Rule 91 issue, and I, as a result, don't want to take a position that may be inconsistent with a Rule 91 request at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Court's information, we join in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Also, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm -- although I have been informed at the break that there might be a reservation by the Defence on this point, it is kind of unusual at this point but I have no problem to defer the admission of those statements until the end of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we need a practical basis to work on. Of course, the Chamber will have to know what is and what is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for practical purposes we could start working on the basis of as if these statements were admitted, but the reservation is there by all three Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with that, Your Honour. The reason I took the position is in light of the attestation and if there is an subsequent issue, and I have a good faith basis at this point to believe there may be a question, I'm reserving my position on it, but I agree wholeheartedly with your position, Your Honour. We should just proceed as if they had been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although it is all still a mystery, of course, to us, but we have to live with that. That's our position. Mr. Waespi, there is an -- I would say especially in the present circumstances, usually the statements are shown on the screen, the witness then confirms that he has signed them and that these are the statements he has given and has reviewed. You've not done that. Nevertheless, of course, the Chamber would like to know exactly to what the witness gave his attestation. So, therefore, I prefer that the copies given to the witness be shown to the Chamber so that we can see to what he actually attested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps with the assistance of the usher. And then, of course, at a later stage, I would like that have the signed copy of the last statement on the screen as well or be given a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the last one is already there in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I don't know whether have you any other copies. I'd like to put these in the hands of the Madam Registrar, hard copies, in front of the witness when he attested to these statements. If have you any spare copies left for the witness, I don't know whether you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I only have my copies but perhaps we can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find ourselves in a little bit of an unusual situation, in which -- of course, the Chamber wants to proceed with the necessary caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe if I'm showing the witness excerpts from his witness statements and there will be very few, certainly in the first hour, we can put it on to the screen or I can read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to read out ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also can be put on the ELMO, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that on the basis of the 65 ter numbers, Madam Registrar could always put them on the screen. Apart, perhaps, from the last one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The 92 ter summary has kind of a different connotation at this point in time, but I think it might still be valuable for the public listening to make this two-minute information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. I do understand that more than usual time will be spent on the examination-in-chief with this witness. So if you have a short summary that would be good to give a context. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I have no papers in front of me, I would like to have a piece of paper where I can note down or am I suppose to receive the papers later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What papers? You mean your own statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, or any other paper that I will relate to. Otherwise, I will have to take notes while we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see, there always is a possibility for you to have the statements. Often only one line will be read. Let's proceed and we'll see. If you feel the need to look at your statements, then we'll find a copy somewhere, or most likely we'll put it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll just take some notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is fine for you to take any notes if you think it would assist you. However, you are not supposed to use any other documents. So start with a clean paper and then whatever you write down to focus your attention on, that's fine. But no other papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness was an operations officer and later monitor and team leader of the European Commission Monitoring Mission, ECMM, teams based in the Knin area from 28 July 1995 until 27th November. During Operation Storm, on 4th and 5th August 1995, he witnessed the shelling of Knin and observed the firing of multiple rocket systems. Witness Liborius personally observed crime incidents within the Krajina during the weeks following the shelling. They include looting, burning of houses, farms and property, as well as destruction of livestock by HV troops and special police. The witness talked to soldiers who explained to him why they were looting. The incidents are reported in various documentation and reports prepared by the witness. The witness, in his capacity as an ECMM official met with two of the accused, Ante Gotovina and Ivan Cermak on a number of occasions between August and October 1995 and raised with both the human rights violations ECMM observed. That's the brief, I guess, undisputed - or perhaps even disputed - summary of Witness 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, we just heard from this brief introduction that you were part of ECMM in August 1995 in the Krajina. Can you tell us what the job, the purpose of ECMM was in the Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: The purpose of the ECMM was to operating under a mandate signed by the six presidents early on during the war to monitor and report on political, military, human rights, economic and other relevant matters, observing and reporting through a structure of teams, coordination centres, regional centres, up to the headquarters of ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many teams were operational in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: In the RSK, the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina, there was a regional centre, RC Knin, abbreviated, it had a number of teams. It had a number of coordination centres under which it had teams, and in the Krajina area between, if we include Sector North and Sector South, in the total we would have between six, seven, up until nine teams, depending on -- on the situation and the organisational structure. The organisation was adopted to the -- to the changing situation on the ground throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was your role within the ECMM structure you have just outlined?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Initially, when I was assigned to the RC Knin, the Regional Centre in Knin, I was designated as an operation officer, and I also served as a team leader. Later on, I had various positions in the ECMM organisation, including in the Regional Centre in Zagreb, and later on, in the headquarters, ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We already heard a summary from me, but can you tell the Court when exactly you arrived in the Krajina and when you left the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I arrived in the late July in 1995 and I left Krajina in late November, 27, 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. Now very, very briefly, did the structure and the mandate of ECMM change with the fall of the RSK around 4th and 5th August 1995?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: The mandate stayed unchanged. It was a very broad mandate. But, of course, the structure was, over the weeks to follow and the month, adjusted. Some of the teams were given new areas of responsibility. Some team structures were added. It was a dynamic process, until the fall of -- or the autumn, well into autumn of 1995 where the RC Knin, the Regional Centre in Knin, was merged in the RC Zagreb structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could have 65 ter 5430. This is a well known photo of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Liborius, where were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like just to inquire with the parties, especially with the Defence teams, you have referred to Rule 91 and you have made a reservation as far as admission of evidence is concerned. As I said before, it is, of course, not known to the Chamber what causes you to refer to Rule 91. That also means that the Chamber could not act proprio motu under Rule 91(A). Nevertheless, if the Defence teams who have not made an application under Rule 91(A) consider that this would be appropriate to do, then, of course, the Chamber would have to perhaps hear a bit more in private session for the reasons so that we'll give, if need be, the -- that we could deal with a warning as provided for in Rule 91(A). It's a situation which does not often appear but the Chamber wants to see whether any consequences already at this moment in procedural terms should be attached to the reservation earlier expressed by all three Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand from that short conversation with Mr. Misetic during the break that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very careful not to discuss the substance of any matter in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly. Because obviously my examination-in-chief will be different if we continue without the admission of these statements, and certainly before we finish tonight I would like to know if I can be given any indication of where it's going. And so without the presence of the witness perhaps we can discuss the specificity of the Defence`s reference to this rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would be happy to do it, Your Honour. I also think it would be wise to do it outside the presence of the witness at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Liborius, I would like to ask you to leave the courtroom briefly so that we can deal with a procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a matter that can be discussed in public, because it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My preference would be in private session, Your Honour, only on the basis that obviously outside people could, in theory, pass information or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of course, I need to know by the end of, I think, today whether the 92 ter application still stands or whether -- which I'll -- prepare to elict all the evidence live from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the inconvenience which is there. If finally, the Chamber would not admit 92 ter statements, we might be in a situation that it doesn't make much sense to elicit, but let's -- let's live with this uncertainty for this moment, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think we left off, Mr. Liborius --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, first of all, thank you for your patience. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We left off where we wanted to go into the morning of the 4th of August, 1995, and I believe I had asked that 65 ter 5430 be retrieved. That's a photo of Knin. Where were you, Mr. Liborius, on the 4th of August, in the early morning hours?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I was working in my accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could blow up the upper left part where we see two markings, A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you mark this photograph, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Could we tilt the photo, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But tilting you mean what, to enlarge it --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: To turn it around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To have north on the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 90 degrees, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that the way you want it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: There's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Surprise me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right, yeah. Yes, I did print the A and B, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you let me know what A means and what B means?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: B is my accommodation, where I was working in the morning hours. And A is the RC Knin, the Regional Centre Knin building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: RC meaning part of ECMM?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You were in the accommodation in B. Now, what did you observe in the early hours of the 4th of August?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I was awake and I was working, and I observed by hearing the impact of heavy artillery fire, and I looked out of the window and I could see heavy smoke from some of the first impacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you observe the impacts?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Once I got out of the -- the building, I could observe impacts to the south in the direction of south, down at the -- the Tvik factory. And I could hear the impacts of heavy artillery in different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there heavy artillery nearby where you were observing the events?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: At that time, in the early morning hours, I judged the -- the closest impacts to be down south of me in and around the Tvik area, but I quickly focussed on getting my personal belongings and my emergency gear and rush up to the -- the Regional Centre, the RC house. And the impacts were heard around in the -- in the area. That's the best description I can give.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a time you conducted a crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: There was -- if I may, for the clarity, explain what I did in the morning hours. Once I had moved up to the Regional Centre, the RC house, we established the ordinary routines of observation from the house, we observed the shelling throughout the -- the morning hours, the day, and the closest impact, I gather that was your previous question, was in the grass fields to the south-west of the -- of the building indicated by A, and I conducted in some of the subsequent days the crater analysis of some of the craters I saw there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall how many craters you saw there?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I saw a couple of craters that were clearly visible of heavy artillery impacts. Some of those I believed I had seen from the operations room in the RC house. By their distinct impact, they left fragmentation marks on the buildings. If you imagine just below the A, there were parked cars and the facades of the house received the shrapnel, the shrapnels from the artillery impacts. The closest impact was about 40, 50 metres of the RC building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you say that the closest impact of these artillery shots were 40 to 50 or -- within the RC building?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: To the south-west of the RC building, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In an area you had described as grass fields.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: The -- the terrain just where the marking A is, there was a -- a dirt and grass field at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your assessment at that time, and your knowledge, was there a military target nearby where you saw these artillery impacts?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I believe that the closest military target would perhaps be the -- the Knin police station, in the line of fire there. But there were no, to my knowledge at least, military targets in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how far away was the police station?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: Roughly 700 metres, 800 metres or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you told us you conducted a crater analysis. What were your findings in relation to source of fire, direction of fire, if you were able to find something out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask for foundation as to the date, when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When did you conduct the crater analysis?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: It's on the screen still blinking here. I conducted the crater analysis a couple of days later, when the ground was still fresh, and my observations indicated that the shelling had been conducted from a direction up north-west -- north-east, sorry, of our location. I think I measured an angle or bearing to the firing position within the 60 or so degrees, meaning up in the mountains area, east of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe you earlier told us that you saw a couple of impacts, and me personally in English I'm never sure what couple means, does it mean two or more. Can you be more specific about how many impacts you saw on that grass field?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS
utterances.text: I remember that I did -- there were two good craters that I could conduct crater analysis on and there were, I mean, a host of other craters. You should remember that, at that time a few days after when you were able to move around, there were many impacts, and I focussed on some of the craters that were clearly, marked clearly. They bore the -- the clear imprints, so that the quality of the crater analysis would be as good as possible. But there were impacts, many, many, impacts. Buildings and in the dirt and -- but not all of those are, so to speak, of a -- of a distinct quality so as to allow a precise crater analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go to a document. This is it 65 ter 5415.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was part of your duties as operational officer to draw reports, Mr. Liborius? And before you answer and before we move into this new area --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the previous exhibit could be -- could be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections. Aerial photograph marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit number P798.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P798 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, I am looking at the clock and see that we have two and a half minutes left. I leave it to you whether your next subject is such that we could cover it in such a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps it would be better to adjourn for the day. Mr. Liborius, before we adjourn, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak to anyone, whoever it is, about the testimony you have already given today, or the testimony still to be given the days to follow. Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Madam Registrar, would that be in this same courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to check in which courtroom we'd like to see you back. The parties will be informed about it. We'll check that on the basis of the Court calendar. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of September, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
